A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Population Transformer work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched across the revised organization.

before.justification: v1 reports original intracranial decoding experiments, efficiency and generalization studies, ablations, and analyses of learned connectivity and attention.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds experiments with alternative temporal encoders, a fine-tuned Brant comparison, scalp-EEG evaluation, and a reconstruction-only ablation. The EEG comparison scores attributed to earlier works are distinguished from these original results.

M1.justification: The transformer backbone, frozen temporal embeddings, two discrimination objectives, channel replacement procedure, and downstream fine-tuning remain. The ensemble encoding explicitly described in v2 was already depicted as sequence position in v1 Figure 1. Additional encoders and EEG inputs exercise the existing modular method without establishing a new algorithm.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates movie-watching intracranial recordings on four auditory-linguistic tasks. v2 retains this coverage and adds TUEG pretraining and TUAB scalp-EEG pathological-versus-normal classification, which the paper labels seizure detection. This adds a distinct recording modality, population, and task.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds fine-tuned Brant and removes the single-channel BrainBERT comparison row. Table 2 adds comparisons with BIOT and LaBraM using scores explicitly attributed to their original works. Deep NN also joins the sample- and compute-efficiency comparisons in v2 Figures 4–5, where v1 Figures 3–4 showed only Linear and the two PopT variants.

E3.justification: The added EEG evaluation uses 21 channels, excludes task subjects from pretraining, and reports balanced accuracy alongside ROC-AUC. New configurations use TOTEM for intracranial data and Chronos/TS2Vec for EEG. The channel-count sweep expands from 1–30 to 1–50 channels, while the original splits and training-step budgets in Appendix A remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Table 3 adds a reconstruction-only pretraining control beyond v1's added-reconstruction-loss ablation. The channel-count sensitivity analysis is extended to 50 channels. The existing loss/position ablations, held-out-subject study, pretraining-subject scaling, frozen-model analyses, and interpretability studies are retained.

E5.justification: v2 adds means and standard deviations across five random seeds for the EEG experiments in Table 2 and Figure 2b. Subject-level standard-error reporting remains for the intracranial experiments. No increase in repeated runs for the retained experiments is stated.

E6.justification: The original BrainBERT PopT AUROC means remain 0.69, 0.84, 0.86, and 0.89. v2 adds TOTEM/Brant results, EEG results, reconstruction-only scores, and additional scaling and efficiency entries. Table 2 reports PopT+TS2Vec AUROC of 0.8907 alongside quoted BIOT and LaBraM values of 0.8815 and 0.9162. Reported PopT pretraining time also changes from four to two days.

T1.justification: The mathematical substance remains the two discrimination tasks and their summed binary-cross-entropy objective. v2 replaces explicit BCE expansions with prose and expands position-encoding notation. These are expository changes; neither version provides theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add the claim that PopT provides a computationally lightweight, more interpretable alternative with competitive performance against end-to-end methods. The title, abstract, and conclusion broaden the demonstrated scope from intracranial activity to multiple neural modalities and temporal encoders, while retaining the original decoding and interpretability contributions.

C2.justification: The limitations change substantially: v1 emphasizes unavailable comparable intracranial datasets and computational obstacles to end-to-end comparisons; v2 emphasizes dependence on meaningful spatial coordinates, individual brain variability, and difficulty identifying functional channels with low-SNR recordings. v2 also adds an explanation linking the Brant comparison to spatial aggregation and discusses potential geophysical and climate applications.

D1.justification: v2 adds temporal-embedding dimensions and parameter, hardware, and compute tables in Appendices A–B. It revises pretraining time from four to two days but removes the 80-CPU-core/700-GB memory disclosure, the explicit 500 ms temporal threshold, and subject identities for the pretraining-subset study. Core optimizer, schedule, split, and code-access information remains.

R1.justification: The related-work structure and novelty argument for modular aggregation across variable channel layouts largely remain. v2 adds references for Chronos, TS2Vec, TUEG, BERT, and aggregation approaches, and removes the Nejedly and Islam references associated with the old limitations. Comparisons with already-cited end-to-end models become explicit empirical positioning.

P1.justification: Beyond the new experiments, v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, existing method explanation, discussion, and conclusion, and condenses interpretability descriptions and captions. It reorganizes the loss explanation, changes the title and terminology, and adds a compute appendix while renumbering retained appendices.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn with separate objective panels and a detailed temporal-encoder pipeline. Table 1 is reorganized by encoder, and new EEG, parameter, and compute tables and a summary bar chart are added. Existing plots receive changed axes, legends, grouping, and placement within a new conference layout; the appendix connectivity and frozen-model graphics are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for encoder/modality generality and its missing end-to-end comparisons through additional encoders, scalp-EEG evaluation, and the Brant comparison. Five-seed EEG reporting and the reconstruction-only control further strengthen the evidence while preserving the original results. EEG competitors remain partly indirect comparisons, and some reproducibility details are lost, but the gains in empirical support and applicability are substantial.
